and that the police would soon have him in their grasp again. I
was wrong, however, Mr. Holmes, for he has never been seen since.
The police have made every effort to trace him, but without
success. The coronet is gone, and so also is my son.  And now I
turn to you, Mr. Holmes, to know whether you can help me in this
most deplorable business."  Mr. Holder sank back into his chair,
completely overwhelmed by his troubles.


"'That you may get away, or perhaps that you may conceal what you
have stolen,' said I. And then, realising the dreadful position
in which I was placed, I implored him to remember that not only
my honour but that of one who was far greater than I was at
stake; and that he threatened to raise a scandal which would
convulse the nation. He might avert it all if he would but tell
me what he had done with the three missing stones.

"That is the question which we have to answer," said Holmes.  "But
before we proceed further, I should like to have a look at the
coronet itself. I would also ask you to give me the exact
measurements of the missing gold corner, with the number and size
of the stones which it contained."
"That is the question which we have to answer," said Holmes. "And
now, Mr. Holder, I think that I will go and see this coronet
myself. I will take a cab to your house and examine it. Let me
have the address."

Mr Holder scribbled it down for him.

"And now, Mr. Holder," said Holmes, rising, "I should wish you
to examine this case with the utmost care. It is most important
that you should do so. Do you notice anything peculiar about it?"

"It is a very handsome case, I admit, though I have not given it
more than a superficial glance."

"It is important to look into such things carefully. Let me know
if you discover anything amiss."

"I will certainly do as you desire."

"And now I will get to work upon this case of yours."

Mr Holder departed, leaving Holmes and me to discuss it.

"That is the question which we have to answer," said Holmes. "And
now, Mr. Holder, I think that I have all that I need. I shall
take the liberty of calling upon you to-morrow morning at
Streatham, and I shall then perhaps bring you some news
which may serve to make your present anxiety somewhat less
painful."

"That is the question which we have to answer," said Holmes. "And
now, Mr. Holder, I think that you have told me all that you know.
I shall now proceed to my own investigations, and I will ask you
to accompany me to the scene of the crime, since I am better
able to judge of the possibilities of the situation if I can see
the room and the surrounding objects with my own eyes. We will
start at once. I would suggest that you bring with you this
damaged coronet, as it may possibly give us some additional
information."

"That is the question which we have to answer," said Holmes. "Now,
let us consider the facts. You awoke, you say, about two, and you
heard a window close. Then you heard footsteps in the next room.
You rushed in and found your son there with the coronet in his
hands. He was trying to bend it back into shape, and he dropped
it when you appeared. This is all very natural, is it not? Your
son, having spent the evening in the company of Sir George
Burnwell, who may well have had some knowledge of the precious
jewel, conceived the idea of possessing himself of it. He
probably had some vague idea of its value and wished to raise
money by its sale or by pledging it. He would have chosen the
night for his enterprise, and the method of removing the gems
would be to break off one of the corners. He would then replace
the remainder of the coronet in its case and, in his haste to
escape, would fail to see that his crime was detected before he
could leave the room."

"But how could he know about the jewel?"

"That is not yet clear," said Holmes, though I have some
conjectures upon the matter. It would require very much
investigation to settle that point."

"I am anxious only for the whereabouts of the jewels."

"That I hope shortly to obtain for you. I shall proceed now to
the house at Streatham. I shall want your aid, Mr. Holder. You
must bring the coronet to me."

"But the police--?"

"The police can wait. I shall want to examine the coronet
carefully in my own rooms."

"Very well," said Mr Holder, rising and preparing to go.

"One moment," said Holmes, glancing at his watch. "There is one
thing more which I should like to know. You say your son told you
that he must have 200 pounds or he could not show his face at his
club. Did he mention the name of the club?"

"Yes--the Diogenes Club."

"Excellent. Thank you. You may now go. I have already dispatched
a messenger to the police, that they may take my instructions
later in the day. We can have no more time to waste."

Mr Holder left, and Holmes and I set to work upon our preparations
at once.
"Precisely. And if it were guilty, why did he not invent a lie?
His silence appears to me to cut both ways. There are several
singular points about the case. What did the police think of the
noise which awoke you from your sleep?"

"They considered that it might be caused by Arthur's closing his
bedroom door."

"A likely story! As if a man bent on felony would slam his door
so as to wake a household. What did they say, then, of the
disappearance of these gems?"

"They are still sounding the planking and probing the furniture
in the hope of finding them."

"Have they thought of looking outside the house?"

"Yes, they have shown extraordinary energy. The whole garden has
already been minutely examined."

It was a detached house of red brick, two stories high, standing
in its own grounds, with a small lawn and a few clumps of
evergreen shrubs in front of it. A carriage-drive, edged with
gravel, swept round in front of the house, and there was a stable
and a coach-house to the side. Holmes examined all these points
with a keen eye, and then we passed through the front garden into
the hall. As we entered it Holmes stopped abruptly and turned
pale. "What is this?" he asked in a whisper. "I thought so!" He
pointed at the ground, which was covered with a broad expanse of
white paint, smeared with splashes and blotches of dark blood.

"The police have been here!" I exclaimed.

"Yes, it was this that made me think that the matter must be more
complex than it appeared. You mentioned paint stains upon the
pavement in Baker Street. This is the same stain. It appears
that Mr. Alexander Holder was a more energetic man than I had
conceived."

It was a large, comfortable house, standing back some distance from
the road, with a well-kept lawn and some fine trees in front of
it. Holmes examined the outside of the house with the keenest
interest, and several times he caused us to return to some
particular point which he wished to study more closely. Finally,
he led us back to the door, and, after a careful scrutiny of the
bell-pull and the steps, he walked round to the side of the
house, and there, after a thorough inspection of the door which
opened into the kitchen, he led us away again to the front. As
he stood upon the step he gave utterance to his thoughts in a
half-whisper.

"There is something curious about this house," said he; "there
is something curious about the way in which this house is built.
The line of windows runs horizontally, except at the end, where
it is vertical. It suggests something to me--I can hardly tell
what. I could almost imagine that the house had once been
divided, and that this is but the joining of two properties.
That would certainly account for the slight difference in
architectural design."


It was a detached house, two-storied, and of a somewhat old-fashioned
pattern, standing back a little from the road and shaded by a
magnificent beech-tree. As we approached, a pretty, fluffy-haired
dog bounded out to greet us, followed by a young lady clad in
mourning, who came running from the house. It was Miss Mary Holder,
and, though I had only seen her once before, I recognised her at
once from her likeness to her photograph.

It was a large, square, two-storied house, of grey stone, with
a flat roof and long windows. It stood back some distance from the
road, and was screened from it by a well-grown shrubbery. Holmes
surveyed it with a keen eye, walking slowly around it, and
pausing at each window. His inspection was very minute, his eyes
often turning upward to the eaves of the house. After he had
completed his tour of inspection, he called upon the banker to
lead him to the room where the incident had taken place.

Holmes examined the house with the keenest interest, going round
it and gazing up at each window, and even making small
measurements with his cane.  He then took the banker aside and
asked him several searching questions concerning the positions of
the various rooms and the habits of the household.  Finally, he
asked to be shown the dressing-room and the bureau.  Mr. Holder led
the way, unlocking the door with a shaking hand, and Holmes
immediately made a very careful examination of the contents of the
bureau.

Fairbank was a good-sized square house of white stone, standing
back a little from the road. A double carriage-sweep, with a
snow-clad lawn, stretched down in front to two large iron gates
which closed the entrance. On the right side was a small wooden
thicket, which led into a narrow path between two neat hedges
stretching from the road to the kitchen door, and forming the
tradesmen's entrance. On the left ran a lane which led to the
stables, and was not itself within the grounds at all, being a
public, though little used, thoroughfare. Holmes left us standing
at the door and walked slowly all round the house, across the
front, down the tradesmen's path, and so round by the garden
behind into the stable lane. So long was he that Mr. Holder and I
went into the dining-room and waited by the fire until he should
return. We were sitting there in silence when the door opened and
a young lady came in. She was rather above the middle height,
slim, with dark hair and eyes, which seemed the darker against
the absolute pallor of her skin. I do not think that I have ever
seen such deadly paleness in a woman's face. Her lips, too, were
bloodless, but her eyes were flushed with crying. As she swept
silently into the room she impressed me with a greater sense of
grief than the banker had done in the morning, and it was the
more striking in her as she was evidently a woman of strong
character, with immense capacity for self-restraint. Disregarding
my presence, she went straight to her uncle and passed her hand
over his head with a sweet womanly caress.

"You have given orders that Arthur should be liberated, have you
not, dad?" she asked.

"No, no, my girl, the matter must be probed to the bottom."

"But I am so sure that he is innocent. You know what woman's
instincts are. I know that he has done no harm and that you will
be sorry for having acted so harshly."

"Why is he silent, then, if he is innocent?"

"Who knows? Perhaps because he was so angry that you should
suspect him."

"How could I help suspecting him, when I actually saw him with
the coronet in his hand?"

"Oh, but he had only picked it up to look at it. Oh, do, do take
my word for it that he is innocent. Let the matter drop and say
no more. It is so dreadful to think of our dear Arthur in
prison!"

Holmes had returned and stood listening with an amused smile upon
his face to this passionate appeal. When she had finished he
walked up to her, his eyes twinkling.

"Madam," said he, "I think that I can promise you that your
brother shall be out of prison before evening."

She looked at him in amazement. Her uncle had started to his
feet and was staring from one to the other of us with his mouth
agape.

"You think you can prove his innocence?" he asked.

"I think I can prove it."

"But the coronet, the missing gems--how can you explain them?"

"By supposing that the whole thing is not as it seems. Please,
Miss Holder, will you give me some account of how you spent
yesterday?"

Holmes returned at this moment, and the conversation was
interrupted.  He had been making a very careful examination of
the outside of the house, and his demeanour showed that he was
satisfied with the result of his observations.  He had a keen,
penetrating glance, and his face was lit by an expression of
triumph.  "I think that I have found the solution of our
problem," he remarked. "It is a singular one, but I think that I
am justified in saying that we shall have no more trouble with
this missing coronet."
The banker, who had shown some signs of relenting, hardened his
heart again at the sight of his niece's distress.  "It is not a
matter for sentiment, Mary," said he. "The honour of a great
family, the safety of the most precious jewel in the kingdom,
are at stake. It is a great public case, and we cannot allow
private feelings to interfere with our duty to the public."

"But surely, uncle," she cried, "if Arthur were guilty, he would
have run away.  He would not have stayed and allowed himself to
be arrested!"

"That is certainly true," said Holmes, who had been listening
intently to the conversation.  "But it may mean that he knows
that we have evidence which will convict him, and that therefore
escape is useless."

"Oh, but it cannot be!" cried Mary, wringing her hands. "There
is some dreadful mystery, and we shall never find the truth."
The girl's distress was so evident and her manner so
straightforward that I felt that there must be some grounds for
her confidence. Holmes, who had re-entered the room and had been
listening with an amused smile upon his face, now came forward.

"I think that I have already solved the mystery," said he. "I
only await a few details from Mr. Holder, and then I propose to
go straight to the police-station and have the young gentleman
released."

"You think, then, that he is innocent?" exclaimed the banker, in
unfeigned astonishment.

"I am sure of it."

"But the coronet--"

"The coronet was not injured at all when your son had it in his
hands. The injury which you observed had already been done. That
is one of the most remarkable facts in the case. The other is
the complete disappearance of the beryls."

"But how could they have disappeared?"

"Precisely. The point is that they did not disappear from
anywhere in the house. They disappeared from the coronet itself,
and then the coronet itself was placed in a position where it was
certain that Arthur would find it."

Holmes had returned and stood watching her with an expression of
intense interest upon his face.  He had listened to the last
words with an air of deep attention, and now, as she ceased, he
approached her quickly and held out his hand.

"My dear Miss Holder," said he, "I must ask you to give me your
confidence in this matter. You seem to me to be one whose
judgment is quite as sound as your instincts are quick. I would
be glad if you would allow me to look into the affair without
interference on the part of your relatives."

"I have already made up my mind as to what to do, Mr. Holmes,"
said she with a heightened colour. "My uncle has promised me
that I might have a chance of making a suggestion. If the police
are not to be trusted, then I know who is. I intend to engage
you to recover the coronet."

"I shall never let it drop until the gems are found--never, Mary!
Your affection for Arthur blinds you as to the awful consequences
to me. Far from hushing the thing up, I have brought a gentleman
down from London to inquire more deeply into it."

"This gentleman?" she asked, facing round to me.

"No, his friend. He wished us to leave him alone. He is round in
the stable lane now."

Holmes had entered the room while she was speaking. He bowed to
her in his quick, alert way, and then looked keenly at her face
with his sharp, questioning eyes. She bore his scrutiny with
perfect composure.

"I have already explained to Mr. Holder," said he, "that it
appears to me of the highest importance that we should establish
beyond all doubt what became of the missing stones during the
night between Saturday and Sunday. What were you doing, Miss
Holder, during that time?"

"I slept soundly. I never heard a sound."

"Did you see anything remarkable on the morning after?"

"No, I saw nothing."

"And your brother?"

"I do not think that my cousin Arthur saw anything more than I did."

"You were in bed all night?"

"Yes, sir."

"And you never looked out at the window?"

"Why should I?"

"Because I find the mark of a muddy boot on the window-sill
which is entirely inconsistent with the fact that the rest of the
window was perfectly clean. You might well have received a
splash or two of mud on the sill when you were going out into the
garden."

"I was not out in the garden," she said.

"No; but perhaps you might have gone out and then returned without
my noticing it. There was something which made me wish to be
perfectly sure."

"What?"

"That you were not out in the garden in the dark. The marks of
a man's feet were visible, but yours were absent."

"There was no need for me to go out into the garden."

"Then, how do you account for the other marks of feet?"

"I cannot tell."

"I have been looking into details," said Holmes. "I am interested
in the question as to whether there was a person other than
yourself in your own bedroom. I have the clearest proof that
someone went to your room, as the mark of his muddy boot upon
the sill clearly shows. But there is no other evidence that the
window has been opened from the outside. On the other hand, the
mark of his boot is a considerable way from the window-sill,
indicating that the person was not standing immediately in front
of it when he made the mark. That is inconsistent with the
hypothesis that he had just opened it and was about to come into
the room. If he had just entered, and the mark is to be taken as
an index of his position, then he was in the room, which was not
the case. That person could not have been Arthur, nor could he
have been anyone else who entered the room at all, because, if
he had done so, there would have been other marks than those of
the boot. In short, if this evidence was conclusive I should
be obliged to infer that there had been someone else in your
room who, since he had to reach such a height, had been
standing on something. Now, a stool, you know, is a rather
suggestive article. This stool is, if I am not mistaken, a
peculiar one, for I see that it is of a kind which is never
seen anywhere in the house, and so it is probably not the work
of a household servant. Who would be likely to bring such an
article into the house? Is it not obvious? Of course, your
cousin, Arthur. There is only one explanation, as far as I can
see. The missing gems are in your room; and Arthur, having got
into the room, and perhaps wishing to return the jewels without
awakening the family, had been placing them in the drawer, when
his father appeared, caught him in the act, and so caused the
misunderstanding and the whole of this lamentable affair."

Mary made no reply. She was very pale, and she held a trembling
hand to her throat.

"Please show me," said Holmes.

She took the key from her pocket and unlocked the bureau. It
was empty.

"He did not want me to find them," said she, with a sigh.

"I see it all now. But it still leaves something to be desired
in the way of explanation. We must search elsewhere. Please,
Miss Holder, would you be good enough to assist me in this matter?"

"Of course."

She laid her hand upon the bureau and turned it carefully. It
sprung back on its hinges, and a small square cavity was disclosed. In it were the three missing beryls.


Holmes had entered the room while she was speaking. He bowed
slightly to her, and then, turning to the banker, he said: "I
think, Mr. Holder, that we should examine the coronet first. May
I ask you to have the goodness to fetch it?"  The banker went to
his dressing-room and returned with the precious case, which he
handed to Holmes.  Holmes opened the case, and took the coronet
out. He held it up to the light and turned it slowly over.  "A
beautiful thing," he remarked; "but the gold has been much
injured by rough usage. One of the corners, as I see, has been
bent, and there are several scratches.  Are all the stones there?"

"No, sir," replied the banker; "three of the beryls are missing.
They were at the corner which was bent."

"Ah! very interesting.  And now, Miss Holder, would you kindly
take us to the stable lane?"

Holmes had entered the room while she was speaking. He bowed
slightly, and looked at her with his keenly observant eyes.

"I have already explained to your uncle," said he, "that I
intend to examine every detail of this curious case, however
trivial it may appear to be. The lane behind the house is no
exception. It seems to be a very convenient passage from one part
of the grounds to another."

"Yes, that is so," she replied, but her face was very pale,
and I could see that she was deeply agitated.

Holmes had entered the room while she was speaking. He looked
grave and attentive as he listened to her words, and his eyes
were fixed upon her face with an expression of singular
intensity.  He bowed slightly in acknowledgment of her greeting,
but made no answer.

Holmes had reappeared in the doorway.  He was smiling, and his
eyes twinkled.  "Indeed, Miss Holder," said he, "I think that I
have already made a small step towards proving your cousin's
innocence."

"I fully share your opinion, and I trust, with you, that we may
prove it," returned Holmes, going back to the mat to knock the
snow from his shoes. "I believe I have the honour of addressing
Miss Mary Holder. Might I ask you a question or two?"

"Pray do, sir, if it may help to clear this horrible affair up."

"You heard nothing yourself last night?"

"Nothing, until my uncle here began to speak loudly. I heard
that, and I came down."

"You shut up the windows and doors the night before. Did you
fasten all the windows?"

"Yes."

"Were they all fastened this morning?"

"Yes."

"You have a maid who has a sweetheart? I think that you remarked
to your uncle last night that she had been out to see him?"

"Yes, and she was the girl who waited in the drawing-room, and
who may have heard uncle's remarks about the coronet."

"I see. You infer that she may have gone out to tell her
sweetheart, and that the two may have planned the robbery."

"But what is the good of all these vague theories," cried the
banker impatiently, "when I have told you that I saw Arthur with
the coronet in his hands?"

"Wait a little, Mr. Holder. We must come back to that. About this
girl, Miss Holder. You saw her return by the kitchen door, I
presume?"

"Yes; when I went to see if the door was fastened for the night I
met her slipping in. I saw the man, too, in the gloom."

"Do you know him?"

"Oh, yes! he is the green-grocer who brings our vegetables round.
His name is Francis Prosper."

"He stood," said Holmes, "to the left of the door--that is to
say, farther up the path than is necessary to reach the door?"

"Yes, he did."

"And he is a man with a wooden leg?"

He examined the windows with the greatest care, measuring the
distances from the ground, and feeling the lintels and the
frames. At one of the windows—that nearest to the stable lane—
he spent a long time, and finally he called up Mr. Holder,
pointing to a small spot of damp on the stonework.

"This," said he, "was caused by the rain last night."

"I daresay it was," said Mr. Holder.

"If this rain had been continuous," Holmes remarked, "this spot
would not have existed. It has only fallen, then, in drops, and
has dried before the next drop fell. I think it is safe to say
that this stone has only been splashed. Is that so?"

"I think it probable."

"Good. Now, Mr. Holder, let us go upstairs to the dressing-room
where the coronet was kept."

He walked swiftly round the room, examining with minute care the
various articles which lay upon the tables and the mantelpiece.
Finally, he took up the empty coffee-pot, and, turning it upside
down, he shook it, rattling the grounds which were still left
inside it. "There seems to be something missing," he remarked,
putting it down again. "It is quite evident that our little
problem will not be very easily solved."

He examined the windows with great care, and I observed that he
looked particularly at the hinges and at the framework of the
windows, especially those upon the ground-floor. Then he went
round to the tradesmen's entrance, and scrutinized that also with
equal care.  After that, he walked up the lawn, and examined the
gates. Finally, he returned to the house, and asked to be taken to
Mr. Holder's bedroom.

He walked swiftly round the room, examining with minute care the
walls, the floor, and the ceiling. The young lady and her uncle
watched him in silent amazement.  He made several notes in his
book, and then, without a word, walked out to the garden, the
young lady following.  Mr. Holder remained in the room, overwhelmed
by the turn which events had taken.

He examined with great care the whole of the windows on the ground
floor, measuring the distance from the ground to the sill, and
testing the strength of the fastenings.  He then went round to the
back of the house and inspected the kitchen entrance as well as
the tradesman's path.  Finally, he returned to the front, and,
after a careful scrutiny of the doors and windows, led the way
upstairs, followed by Mr. Holder and his niece.

He walked swiftly round from one to the other, pausing only at
the large one which looked from the hall onto the stable lane.
This he opened and made a very careful examination of the sill
with his powerful magnifying lens. "Now we shall go upstairs,"
said he at last.

The banker's dressing-room was a plainly furnished little
chamber, with a grey carpet, a large bureau, and a long mirror.
Holmes went to the bureau first and looked hard at the lock.

"Which key was used to open it?" he asked.

"That which my son himself indicated--that of the cupboard of the
lumber-room."

"Have you it here?"

"That is it on the dressing-table."

Sherlock Holmes took it up and opened the bureau.

"Then I must," said Holmes; and taking a pair of pliers from his
pocket he proceeded to snap the golden corner from the coronet.
It broke with a sharp snap, and then, as Holmes held it up, we all
of us saw that there were three small, almost invisible cracks
at the back of each of the stones, which showed that they had
been cemented in, not set in the ordinary way. Holmes smiled
triumphantly. "It only needed a little pressure to detach them,"
said he.

"But how were they replaced?" asked the banker.

"The point is that they were never removed," said Holmes; "they
only appeared to be." He held up the coronet and the broken
corner. "You see that the inner surface is roughened. Now,
observe." He held the broken corner to the other. "It fits
perfectly, does it not? The fractured edges coincide, and the
three stones are cemented into the corner. Do you remember
hearing of a mysterious affair at the house of Sir George Burnwell
some few years ago? I am confident that this case is a similar
one. I suggest that one of Sir George's friends, who must be
known to Arthur, had pledged the coronet to his firm; that the
pledge came due on Monday, but that, before his friend was in a
position to redeem it, some unforeseen circumstance demanded
50,000 pounds in ready money. This he obtained from your son; and
in order that his friend should not forfeit the coronet he had
the ingenious idea of simulating its destruction. The gems would
be quite safe in his hands for a while. In the meantime he
would induce your son to steal the coronet, thus diverting
suspicion from himself and his friend. With the return of the
coronet he would hope to recover his money. In this theory you
will observe that nothing is wanting but the appearance of the
gems."


"Then I must," said Holmes, taking up a small penknife. "I wish
to compare the fracture with that upon the other fragment."

He delicately inserted the blade into the gold, and with a
gentle twist snapped off the corner. The two pieces fitted
perfectly.

"You see," said he, holding them up, "that the fracture is exactly
the same in both cases. It is quite clear, therefore, that the
missing gems were never removed from the coronet. It was simply
bent so that the corner was hidden, and the jewel looked as if it
were missing."

"But how could any such slight thing have deceived me?" cried the
banker in amazement.

"I do not say that it was, save in the dim light and to one who
was filled with the emotions which were working upon you. With
your nerves shattered by the events of the night, it was natural
that you should look upon it with eyes which were incapable of
seeing the real facts. If Arthur were innocent, it would be a
simple enough matter to prove it."


"Then I must," said Holmes, taking a pair of pliers from his
pocket. "You see, it is quite easy. It is only necessary to
twist it gently to one side and then pull. Now observe, there are
three beryls loose. This is exactly the way in which the other
three were removed."


"Then I must do it myself," said Holmes, taking up a small
hammer and carefully breaking off the corner. "You see that it
corresponds exactly to the fracture in the other piece. It is
quite clear, therefore, that the coronet has been broken at two
different times. Now observe this. The three stones which are
missing are the largest and finest in the coronet, are they not?"

"Yes, undoubtedly," said the banker, looking at the shattered
gems in mute amazement.

"And, what is of the utmost importance, observe that the three
stones which have been taken are all of them loose stones, while
none of those which remain are loose."

"So they are!"

"Could this be merely coincidence?"

"Certainly not. This is most important."

"It is more than that; it is conclusive. The coronet has been
tampered with twice. The thief knew that the stones were loose.
It is inconceivable that they should have fallen out by
themselves. They would never have been so neatly extracted unless
the whole thing had been planned."

"Then I must do it myself," said Holmes, taking the coronet in
his hand. With a sudden sharp blow he wrenched the gold corner from
its place, and there, in his hand, were three superb beryls. He
laid them down upon the table beside the other precious stones.

"Mr. Holder," said he, "you can now see that the fracture of the
coronet corresponds exactly to the corner which has been broken
off. Your son was not trying to steal the gems; he was trying to
repair the coronet. It is a pity that in so doing he did not
trust you with the true reason of his action, but you must admit
that his innocence is now clearly established."

"My dear sir, I should never have believed it. I am so overjoyed!
But if he did not steal the gems, who did?"

"Exactly. That is the next question which we have to answer. What
do you think, Miss Holder?"

"I know not what to say, sir, I am so happy, so overjoyed."

"Well, then, consider that this case is still under investigation
and that we are about to attempt a solution of it. Remember how
strange a coincidence it was that your son should pick this
particular night to mend the coronet, why he should have chosen
to do this, and why he should have adopted this extraordinary
method of doing it. He did not tell you. Why not?"

"Indeed, that is so, Mr. Holmes," cried the banker. "That is the
puzzle."

"We shall find out," said Holmes; "for one thing is clear, that
there was some reason that made him act with such terrible
secrecy and that his guilt or innocence should hang upon the
clear establishment of that reason."

"He was always a strange fellow," said the father, stroking his
chin thoughtfully. "I did not understand him, not at all."

"There is an answer to all this in his strange conduct," said
Holmes. "I am sure of it."

"Then I will." Holmes suddenly bent his strength upon it, but
without result. "I feel it give a little," said he; "but, though
I am exceptionally strong in the fingers, it would take me all my
time to break it. An ordinary man could not do it. Now, what do
you think would happen if I did break it, Mr. Holder? There would
be a noise like a pistol shot. Do you tell me that all this
happened within a few yards of your bed and that you heard
nothing of it?"

"I do not know what to think. It is all dark to me."

"But perhaps it may grow lighter as we go. What do you think,
Miss Holder?"

"I confess that I still share my uncle's perplexity."

"Your son had no shoes or slippers on when you saw him?"

"He had nothing on save only his trousers and shirt."

Holmes went to the window and examined it with his lens. Then he
opened it and looked out. "There is a curious mark on the sill,"
he observed. "It looks like the scratch of a shoe, and it is
rather broad and deep. It is made by no ordinary shoe, but by a
shoe with a very broad, thick sole, such as is worn by country
people. It appears to have been made by someone standing on the
window-sill outside, and scraping the sole along it as they got
in. Now, let us look at the other windows. I think that we can
come to some conclusion on this matter if we find other traces of
the same kind."

Holmes went to the window and examined it with his lens. Then he
opened it and stepped out onto the sill. Again he inspected the
outside of the window frame with the utmost care. "It is a very
old-fashioned lock," he remarked, "and easily opened. The
window is over the stable lane, which is a public thoroughfare.
One might easily pass this house without being observed." He then
went to each of the other windows, giving them the same scrutiny.
Finally, he walked round the house once more, and then returned
to us with his hands in his pockets, his brows knitted, and an
expression of profound thought upon his face. He looked at the
cracked corner of the coronet, and then at the window, and then
he suddenly burst out laughing.

"The mystery is solved!" he cried. "I have it all. It was
perfectly clear to me the moment I saw that the corner had not
been broken off, but had been cut off.

Holmes went to the window and examined it with his lens. "How
long have you had that flower-pot, Mr. Holder?" he asked.

"Since last spring."

"It is large and heavy?"

"Very."

"How is it fixed?"

"It stands on the window sill."

"And is there anything behind it?"

"Nothing but the wall."

"Look here!" Holmes pointed to a crack which extended for
several inches up the wall just behind the flower-pot. "Do you
observe this crack? It is merely a very fine one, but it is
certainly there. Now, let us get our lens again."

He looked through it for a long time. "You must have had
trouble with your flower-pot before now," said he.

"Never."

"Well, I have it now. It has fallen, or been pushed, from the
window sill, leaving the marks of its fall on the wall. But,
more than that, it has recently been replaced, and that crack has
been carefully plastered over with a cement which is still wet.
We are in luck, for it has not yet had time to harden, so that
we can find the missing stones."

"Wonderful!" I exclaimed.

"The cement must be very sticky," remarked the young lady.

"Precisely, so that if the three stones were thrown here they
would have stuck fast," cried Holmes.

Holmes went to the window and examined it with his lens. Then he
walked round the room, making a careful scrutiny of every object
in it. Finally, he took up the coronet and carried it to the
window. "I am now going to ask you," said he, "to look at the
back of the coronet and to observe that the gold is considerably
worn just where the missing stones were."

The banker looked and nodded.

"And yet," continued Holmes, "the three stones were not removed
until after the coronet was brought to the house. This shows that
the theft was not an ordinary one. The thief must have had some
previous knowledge of the coronet, and he must have done it in a
very quiet, gentle way, so as not to make a noise. I do not think
that this is the work of an ordinary thief."

"What, then, is it?"

"The work of someone who was familiar with the coronet, and who
knew that the stones were loose. And that would be Sir George
Burnwell," said Holmes.


Holmes went to the window and examined it with his lens. "How
high is this window from the ground?" he asked.

"About five feet."

"And the ground is soft?"

"Yes, it is all flower-beds."

"Then the thief must have left some trace of his footmarks. We
shall look for them."

He went alone, at his own request, for he explained that any
unnecessary footmarks might make his task more difficult. For an
hour or more he was at work, returning at last with his feet
heavy with snow and his features as inscrutable as ever.

"I think that I have seen now all that there is to see, Mr.
Holder," said he; "I can serve you best by returning to my
rooms."

"But the gems, Mr. Holmes. Where are they?"

"I cannot tell."

The banker wrung his hands. "I shall never see them again!" he
cried. "And my son? You give me hopes?"

"My opinion is in no way altered."

"Then, for God's sake, what was this dark business which was
acted in my house last night?"

He left us then, and we returned to our own house, wondering
what this new development might mean.  The banker was clearly
relieved by Holmes' confidence, but Mary remained deeply troubled,
her eyes following Holmes' departing figure with a mixture of
hope and apprehension.  The entire episode left a profound sense
of unease and anticipation hanging heavy in the air.
He left us, and we returned to our gloomy task of considering
what was to be done. Mary, however, had regained a little of her
composure, and, with her usual practical good sense, she set
herself to arrange matters so that the household should be as
little disturbed as possible by the impending investigation. It
was agreed that we should say nothing to Arthur, that we should
not let him see that we had any clue to his innocence, since
that might possibly make him more intractable. Meanwhile, I sent
a telegram to my partner, informing him of the new turn which
events had taken and of the arrival of Mr. Holmes, so that he
should not be surprised if he heard any rumours of the affair.

He left us, and we descended to the drawing-room, where Miss
Holder was still waiting, her face pale and drawn with anxiety.
She looked at her uncle with her great, dark, appealing eyes,
as though imploring him to spare his son. He seemed to have been
moved by her silent sorrow and her confidence in her brother's
innocence, and he took her hand with a tenderness which showed
how much his love for her and his admiration for her character
had strengthened with the years.

"We shall know more to-morrow, my dear," he said. "I have no
doubt that Mr. Holmes will have got to the heart of the matter
and will be able to clear Arthur of this dreadful accusation."

"Yes, I am sure that he will," she answered, with more hope
in her tone than I had expected to hear.

He left us, and I accompanied my uncle back to the fire, where we
sat in silence until the arrival of Mrs. Charpentier's carriage
announced that it was time for us to return to town.  Mary had
remained in her room since Holmes' departure; and her uncle and
I went out without seeing her.  The whole case was a dark and
enigmatic one, and though Holmes had spoken with confidence, I
felt far from easy in my mind.  His words, however, had inspired
a faint gleam of hope, and I was glad to think that the matter
would be investigated by one whose sagacity was so well known.

He left us, and we drove back to town together.  The banker was
a man of such evident sincerity that it was impossible to doubt
his grief, and I confess that I was filled with a profound
sympathy for him in his distress.  His niece, however, though
equally distressed, seemed to me to be a woman of stronger
character, and her confidence in her cousin's innocence, though
it might be mistaken, was evidently very sincere.  It was a
singular case, and I was eager to hear Holmes' explanation.
It was obvious to me that my companion's mind was now made up
about the case, although what his conclusions were was more than
I could even dimly imagine. Several times during our homeward
journey I endeavoured to sound him upon the point, but he always
glided away to some other topic, until at last I gave it over in
despair. It was not yet three when we found ourselves in our
rooms once more. He hurried to his chamber and was down again in
a few minutes dressed as a common loafer. With his collar turned
up, his shiny, seedy coat, his red cravat, and his worn boots, he
was a perfect sample of the class.

"It is all perfectly clear now," said he, seating himself in his
armchair and stretching out his long legs before the fire. "I
shall be able to tell you everything to-morrow. It is a most
singular case, and one which has afforded me exceptional
opportunities for observation. I think that I have added
something to my collection of methods, and perhaps I have made
one or two deductions which may be useful to us. In any case,
the matter has been interesting."

He spoke with animation, but I noticed that he was very careful
to avoid giving me any clue as to the direction in which his
inquiries were tending. I thought it best, therefore, to leave
him to his own thoughts, and waited patiently until he should
choose to confide in me. I knew that there was no need for haste.
What he had said already had sufficiently whetted my
curiosity, and I felt sure that the explanation which was to
follow would be well worth the waiting for. I took up my book
and endeavoured to settle to it, but my mind kept wandering away
to the remarkable case which had engaged us. How had it ended?
Who had been the true culprit? I lay in bed that night, after
the morning visit from our banker client, turning the whole
matter over and over in my mind, and searching for some other
solution. At last, I hit upon it.

"It is all perfectly clear now. The only difficulty is to
persuade the police that my theory is correct. They are so
prejudiced against young Holder that they are unwilling to look
at the matter in any other light. However, I am certain that I
can prove to you that not only is he innocent, but that the
stones are in safe hands and will soon be recovered."

"I have made some progress. It is certainly a curious case, and
one which presents some features of considerable interest. You
must admit that this is rather an odd thing for a man to do," and
he held up the elastic-sided boot which he had brought with him.

"It is certainly an odd thing to have in one's rooms," said I.

"I think that it might be made even odder," said Holmes, and he
took from his pocket a small paper parcel, from which he extracted
three gems, the very counterparts of those which had been lost
from the coronet.

"The gems are certainly genuine," said I, after a careful
examination.

"Ah! it is a very rare stone, and one which is easy to distinguish
when seen. Now, with your leave, I shall have a look at my notes
before I go on to the next point in my investigation."

"Swimmingly. I have got possession of one of the most important
pieces of evidence. It is not quite what I expected, but it is
something. This boot, for example, is a most useful article. The
sole is of a peculiar construction, and one which is not very
commonly used in this country."

"How did you come across it?"

"It was lying in the stable lane. It was quite fresh, and the
marks upon it made me think that it would be interesting to take
it with me."

"But surely you have some idea?" I exclaimed.

"Patience, my dear fellow! It is possible that I may have to take
a short journey. If I do, I shall certainly be away for a night.
Good-bye! Don't wait up."

He hurried from the room, and I was left to spend a long and
anxious evening, for I knew enough of my friend to be sure that
some dramatic and unexpected development was about to take place.

"Swimmingly. I have seen the green-grocer. I have also seen Sir
George Burnwell. I have also seen the young lady. I think that
I have solved the mystery, Watson, although I have yet to
confront the guilty party with the facts. I rather fancy that
you will find me to be quite right in my conclusions, though
perhaps the sequence of events may strike you as being a little
singular."

"Oh, so so. Nothing to complain of. I have been out to Streatham
since I saw you last, but I did not call at the house. It is a
very sweet little problem, and I would not have missed it for a
good deal. However, I must not sit gossiping here, but must get
these disreputable clothes off and return to my highly
respectable self."

I waited until nearly midnight, but there was no sign of his
return. I had just begun to feel a little anxious when the key
turned in the lock and he entered, looking weary but triumphant.
He held a small, black morocco case in his hand.  He dropped
heavily into his chair and gazed at it with a look of
satisfaction.

"Well, have you got them?" I asked.

"Yes; all three of them."

"And where was the hiding place?"

"Oh, that was the best bit of it," he said with a chuckle. "It
shows how easily we may all be deceived when we have not taken
sufficient trouble to verify the premises. It is so simple that I
am ashamed to think that it should ever have escaped me. There is
one place, and only one place, where a man could conceal a small
object of this kind about him with any degree of security, and
yet leave it always under his own immediate control."

"Where?" I asked.

"In his own boot."

He opened the case and showed me the three gems sparkling upon
their bed of velvet.

"And Arthur?"

"I wish that I had known you would ask me that question," said
Holmes gravely. "Arthur is innocent."

I waited until nearly midnight, but there was no sign of his
return. I had just decided to go to bed when the door opened, and
he stood in the doorway, his features grey with fatigue, but
with triumph in his eyes. He held in his hand a small, black,
morocco case.

"The gems are recovered, Watson," said he, "and young Mr. Holder is
as innocent as I am myself."

"Well?" I cried, eagerly, "but how?"

"That is just what I am about to tell you. But first I must have
a bite of something to eat. I have had nothing since this
morning but that sandwich, and I must confess that it has not
proved a very satisfying meal."

It was nearly midnight before I heard his key in the lock, and
when he entered I perceived that he was not alone. His companion
was a lady, tall and slender, with a face which was beautiful
though pale, and with those dark, expressive eyes which I
associated with the most charming of our recent clients. It was
Miss Mary Holder, and she was even more striking in her evening
dress than she had been in the simpler attire of the morning.

"You may be interested in seeing this, Watson," said Holmes,
with a triumphant smile. He produced a small, velvet-lined case,
and opened it. Within lay three of the finest beryls which it
was ever my fortune to gaze upon.

"What does this mean?" I asked.

"It means, my dear fellow, that my friend Mr. Holder has regained
his jewels and Arthur his freedom."

"You have got them back then?"

"Yes, from the very person who took them."

"But how?" I asked, with considerable curiosity.

"You shall know in good time. I should like to hear our client's
account of this extraordinary affair. Will you tell us about it
yourself, Miss Holder?"

It was late in the evening before he returned. He was in excellent
spirits, and his face was flushed with excitement. He had changed
his clothes, and was once more the Sherlock Holmes of my
acquaintance. He held a small, flat, oblong box in his hand.

"Here are the gems, Watson," said he, opening it. "I had to
resort to a ruse to get them back. Perhaps you would care to
know?"


I waited until nearly midnight, but there was no sign of his
return. I retired to my room, feeling sure that something of
importance was afoot, and that the strange quest in which he
was engaged was nearing its successful end.  My belief proved to
be correct, for it was just past nine o'clock when Holmes
entered, and I could see at a glance that he was in excellent
humour. He laid a small morocco case on the table before him,
opened it, and revealed its contents.

I waited until midnight, but there was no sign of his return, so
I retired to my room. It was no uncommon thing for him to be away
for days and nights on end when he was hot upon a scent, so that
his lateness caused me no surprise. I do not know at what hour he
came in, but when I came down to breakfast in the morning there
he was with a cup of coffee in one hand and the paper in the
other, as fresh and trim as possible.

"You will excuse my beginning without you, Watson," said he, "but
you remember that our client has rather an early appointment this
morning."

"Why, it is after nine now," I answered. "I should not be
surprised if that were he. I thought I heard a ring."

"Well, Mr. Holmes," said he, "have you learned anything yet? Have
you found the gems? Do you know who the thief is?" He spoke in a
low, dull voice, quite different from the passionate exclamations
of the day before.

"I have, I think, solved the mystery, Mr. Holder," replied Holmes,
and, drawing a small, three-cornered piece of cardboard from his
pocket, he placed it upon the table. It was of a dull, grey
colour, with a certain number of very fine lines scratched upon
it. "Do you recognise this?" he asked.

"It appears to be a portion of the cardboard back of a
photograph. The scratches may have some meaning for you, but to
me it is meaningless."

"I beg your pardon, Mr. Holder. It has, I should think, a very
obvious meaning. If I may venture to say so, it is a clue which
should lead straight to the person who possesses the missing
gems."

"Where then do you say that they are?" asked Mary, who had
followed her uncle. "How could anyone find them when the
police, with all their diligence, failed?"

"They are in the possession of your maid Lucy Parr."

"Lucy Parr!" cried both the uncle and the niece together, and
with so much amazement and horror that I could not but
sympathise with their amazement.

"I have had the satisfaction of being able to recover the three
missing beryls, Mr. Holder, and here they are," said Holmes,
producing them from his pocket.

"Well, Mr. Holmes," said he, "have you made any progress?"

"Yes, I think that I have," said Holmes, with his most
reassuring smile. "I have got to the bottom of the matter."

"But the gems, Mr. Holmes, the gems! Have you found them?"

"Yes, I have."

"And where are they?"

"They are here." Holmes pointed to an old boot in the corner.
"I should like you to examine them for yourself. I presume
that this is your property?"

"Yes," said the banker; "this is my boot."

"I found it at the foot of the tradesman's path this morning."

The banker looked at it in astonishment.

"You cannot mean that the gems were in there?"

"I have brought them from there, and I suggest that you examine
them at once."

The banker opened the boot. It contained the three missing
beryls.

"I think that now, Mr. Holder," said Holmes, "that you will
understand this business somewhat better. I wish you to make up
your mind as to your son's guilt or innocence before I lay
further details before you."


"Well, Mr. Holmes," said he, "have you succeeded in discovering
anything concerning my unfortunate son?"

"I have succeeded in discovering the truth, Mr. Holder, and I
think that you will agree with me that it is a very much more
remarkable story than the one which we heard yesterday."

"But the gems?"

"Come what may, Mr. Holder, we shall have them back."

"Then tell me everything. I am so wretched that I hardly know
what I am doing or saying. It is the uncertainty which is so
dreadful."

"I shall tell you exactly what occurred, but you must promise me
to keep a calm mind whatever the explanation may be."

"You can rely upon me."

"Very good. Then I must begin by stating my conviction that
your son is innocent of any crime whatsoever."

"Innocent! If I did not see him myself, Mr. Holmes, with the
coronet in his hands--"

"You saw him with the coronet in his hands, but did you see him
take it? I think that you will agree that, even to the trained
eye, this is not a conclusive proof."

"But, on the other hand, what other explanation is there?" cried
the banker, whose restless spirit was already excited by the
strange statement of my companion.

"I will explain it to you," said Holmes. "It is all rather
subtle, but you will follow me when you have grasped the
explanation. In the first place, it is obvious that the thief
must have planned this robbery with the greatest possible
circumspection. He or she must have studied the conditions under
which your gems were kept, and must have known that there was a
certain danger that the bureau itself might be inspected."

"Well, Mr. Holmes," said he, "have you any news for me? Have you
succeeded in recovering my gems?"  He spoke in a low, dull voice,
quite unlike the excited tones of the previous day.  His eyes were
fixed upon my companion with an almost painful intensity.

"Well, Mr. Holmes," said he, "have you succeeded in recovering
the gems?"

"I have."

The banker looked at my companion with astonishment. "It is
impossible!" he cried. "Where are they?"

"They are here," said Holmes, taking a small morocco case from
his pocket. "I found them this morning."

"You have the coronet?" cried Mr. Holder, springing from his chair.
"My God, what will you charge me?"

"What will you give me, Mr. Holder?"

"I would give my fortune to have them back."

"I am afraid that you must pay a heavy price. But you will pay
it gladly, I am sure. Here is your coronet. The three gems are
replaced, and if you examine them carefully you will find that
they fit perfectly."

"This is indeed it," cried the delighted banker. He examined it
minutely; then, throwing back his head and laughing, he slapped
his hands and shouted, "The gems are there! Holmes, you have saved
my credit and my reputation! But, now tell me what was this
mystery?"

"You must wait for a short time. I must ask you a question or
two more. When I saw the state of the window-sill, and when I
examined the marks upon it, I was very strongly inclined to
think that the thief of the coronet had made his way out of the
window."

"I have no doubt that he did," said Mr. Holder.

"As to how he got in, that is not quite so clear. The house-maid
says that she fastened all the windows last night."

"So she did," said Mary, with conviction.

"Yet there were marks indicating that one at least had been
opened from the outside. It is quite a little problem. But, you
see, I had reason to think that it was not the house-maid."

"How?"

"Because when I came round to the stable-lane this morning I saw
clear indications that two people had been there together the
night before. One had been walking towards the house, and the
other away from it. The one who was going away had a wooden leg.
The one who came to the house was not the house-maid. The marks
were entirely different."

"Yes?"

"I examined the spot with my lens and found that the snow which
had fallen last night was unbroken except for a few marks which
indicated that one person with a wooden leg had passed. He must
have got over the garden wall to avoid the tradesmen's path."

"And the other?"

"The other person, as I have said, went up to the house. You
mention that Lucy Parr, your second housemaid, has a sweetheart.
I found him in the lane and asked him if he had seen her last
night."

"And he said that he had not?"

"Oh, quite otherwise. He confessed to having been near the side
gate to see her. I inquired whether he had noticed anything
unusual, and he said that he had seen her walking alone down the
lane after a man. The man went out by the side gate, but she
waited a long time after him before she came up to the house.
Now it struck me that this was rather late for a lady to be
wandering alone down the lane. I saw, too, the marks of a pair of
boots on the garden path. I found the boots themselves in the
tradesmen's path. The boots are not only a very rare size but have
the peculiarity of being made in the best possible way for silent
walking. They are well covered in snow. They might have come from
any part of the house or garden, but as they were in the path I
naturally expected to find them there."

"But how could she get the gems?"

"Oh, that's the most singular part of the affair. Your son was not
a thief. He only picked up the coronet to look at it. The other
person was waiting in the house. They took the gems and ran off
through the garden."

"And who was it?"

"Sir George Burnwell," said Holmes. "I have the proof here."

He opened his bag and drew out a small phial. "This is a very
powerful and rare perfume. It is the perfume worn by Sir George
Burnwell. I found this phial in his bedroom. I only need mention
that it is a very unusual scent. That is all."

"I do not know what I have done to be so severely tried," said
he. "Only two days ago I was a happy and prosperous man, without
a care in the world. Now I am left to a lonely and dishonoured
age. One sorrow comes close upon the heels of another. My niece,
Mary, has deserted me."

"Deserted you?"

"'My dear uncle,' she writes, 'I have learned from the police
that you intend to charge my cousin, Arthur, with the theft of
the beryls. I cannot believe him to be guilty. I know him to be
innocent. If he is wrongly accused I could not bear to live
under your roof. In the hope that you may yet do justice to him
I have left. Your loving niece, Mary.'"

"'My dearest uncle,' she writes, 'your words of last night have
decided me. If Arthur is innocent, as I know him to be, then
nothing could make me his wife. If he is guilty, then it would be
a base thing for me to remain in your house. So I have gone to
him, and whatever his fate may be I shall share it.'

"Such is the note, Mr. Holmes, and I am left alone in my old
age. All that I had in the world is gone."

"'My dearest uncle,' she writes, 'your words have shown me the
truth. I have been blind, but now I see it all. Arthur is
innocent; you are right to pursue the matter; but I will not
wait to see his name cleared, because I feel that it must
inevitably come out how I have acted in the matter. I have been
the only person who had access to the coronet, and I have
removed the gems for a purpose which I hope may soon be justified.
I shall never see you again, but I shall pray for your health and
happiness. Your loving niece, Mary.'"

"'My dearest uncle,' she wrote, 'I cannot bear to see you suffer
any longer, and I feel that I cannot remain under the same roof
with one who holds such unworthy suspicions of the best and
dearest of men. I have made up my mind to leave at once for
America, where I hope that I shall find such peace of mind as I
can never find in your house. I feel too sure that my cousin
Arthur is innocent, and that you have acted very wrongly toward
him. Pray forgive me if I have been hasty, but I could not
remain to see you treat so unjustly the man whom I love.'

"She has gone, Mr. Holmes. She has gone, and I am left alone!"

The old man bowed his head and sobbed like a child.

"'My dearest uncle,' she writes, 'I feel that I cannot remain
under your roof after what you said to me last night. I can
understand that you should feel bitter against my cousin, but
even though he may be guilty I am sure that he has not deserved
all the harsh words which you have used. It would have been
better, perhaps, if I had married him when he asked me. It is
too late now, but I would do so still were it not that I know how
deeply it would wound your feelings. For that reason alone I have
left your house, and I hope that you will find some way of making
peace with my cousin Arthur. I wish you all happiness, dear
uncle, though I fear that it is not for me to share it.'

"There, Holmes, what do you say to that? Surely such conduct
could only arise from the deepest love and devotion for my boy.
Can there be guilt in such a place?"

"'MY DEAREST UNCLE:--I feel that I have brought trouble upon you,
and that if I had acted differently this terrible misfortune
might never have occurred. I cannot, with this thought in my
mind, ever again be happy under your roof, and I feel that I must
leave you forever. Do not worry about my future, for that is
provided for; and, above all, do not search for me, for it will
be fruitless labour and an ill-service to me. In life or in
death, I am ever your loving,--MARY.'

"What could she mean by that note, Mr. Holmes? Do you think it
points to suicide?"

"No, no, nothing of the kind. It is perhaps the best possible
solution. I trust, Mr. Holder, that you are nearing the end of
your troubles."

"Ha! You say so! You have heard something, Mr. Holmes; you have
learned something! Where are the gems?"

"You would not think 1000 pounds apiece an excessive sum for
them?"

"I would pay ten."

"That would be unnecessary. Three thousand will cover the matter.
And there is a little reward, I fancy. Have you your check-book?
Here is a pen. Better make it out for 4000 pounds."

With a dazed face the banker made out the required check. Holmes
walked over to his desk, took out a little triangular piece of
gold with three gems in it, and threw it down upon the table.

With a shriek of joy our client clutched it up.

"You have it!" he gasped. "I am saved! I am saved!"

The reaction of joy was as passionate as his grief had been, and
he hugged his recovered gems to his bosom.

"There is one other thing you owe, Mr. Holder," said Sherlock
Holmes rather sternly.

"Owe!" He caught up a pen. "Name the sum, and I will pay it."

"Not so fast, Mr. Holder. There is still something to be done.
The police are waiting for us. There is one more person who
should be informed of the facts."

"Who is that?"

"Sir George Burnwell."

"Not so fast. There is one point which still remains obscure.
When I examined the coronet, there was one slight scratch upon
the gold, just where the missing corner had been torn away. That
could hardly have been made by Arthur's fingers, since he left no
mark upon the other portions of the coronet. I have an idea that
we shall soon know how that came there."

"I have already sent a message to the police authorities. He
will be released before evening. I must ask you to wait until
then, Mr. Holder, for I have some other points to clear up
before I can lay the whole story clearly before you."

"I will wait. I will wait with patience, for I am sure that I
shall soon know all. Pray tell me then, what has happened. If it
were not Arthur, who then took the gems?"

"My dear sir," said Holmes, leaning back in his chair and
folding his hands, "I have already made up my mind, but I must
have your sanction before I tell you. I can only do so if you
promise me that you will act strictly in accordance with my
advice."

"Indeed, I would act upon your words as if they were those of an
oracle."

"Good. Then, as to the gems, there is no doubt whatever as to
their whereabouts. They were not stolen, but merely hidden, by
one who would be glad to have them again now that she has learned
the value they possess. The thief was not Arthur, but the
second waiting-maid, Lucy Parr."

"Lucy Parr!" cried the banker, in amazement. "But how came the
stones to be in Arthur's room?"

"Simply because, as I said, she wished him to be suspected of
taking them, but also that they might be restored. She is a girl
who had been led away by some young man, and who feared to have
him suspected, and who believed herself able to secure the safety
of the gems and her own respectability."

"But how was it done?"

"She entered the room while the family was taking coffee and
managed to conceal the gems. The noise which awoke you was
probably the closing of the window which she left open on
entering. She did not see that Arthur was watching, and was
naturally horrified when she heard his name mentioned. Knowing
his wild, reckless ways and his desperate need of money she
thought he must have taken them to pay off his debts."

"And why should she have wished to place the gems in his hands?"

"Because of Sir George Burnwell, and on account of the great
scandal which the loss of the coronet would make."

"But how did Sir George Burnwell come into the business?"

"That, my dear sir, is the most interesting point of all."

"Not so fast, Mr. Holder. There is still something to be done.
There is an innocent man in prison and a guilty woman still at
large."  Holmes paused, his eyes twinkling.  "We must find Lucy
Parr."
"Not so fast, Mr. Holder. We must give the police some little
opportunity of showing their mettle. We must make it appear that
it was they who discovered the thief. I trust that you will be
discreet. A word in your ear, Mr. Holder. I have never yet met
your partner, Mr. Stevenson. Is he a man of strong passions?"

"He is a man of no passions save only avarice."

"A remarkable man. Well, I can promise you that this matter
will not end until you have another story to tell which will be
as surprising as this. Now, with your permission, I will call on
Inspector Baynes. Do you think that there would be any chance of
our getting him round here at once?"

"I will go and ring him up if you like."

"Would it be too much to ask you to telephone also to Sir George
Burnwell? Ask him to step round about midday. I think that you
will find that you have quite a little circle of friends whom
you may wish to meet under my guidance. What do you say to a
pleasant little discussion after lunch, with all the windows
shut?"

"He knows it already. When I had cleared it all up I had an
interview with him, and finding that he would not tell me the
story, I told it to him, on which he had to confess that I was
right and to add the very few details which were not yet quite
clear to me. Your news of this morning, however, may open his
lips."

"For heaven's sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary
mystery!"

"It is so, however. I found her note to you, and I have also
found a letter from Sir George Burnwell to her among her papers.
The two were clearly in correspondence. It was Sir George who
suggested that she should leave your house. She has gone to him,
and you will see her no more. The rest of the mystery is simpler.
Your son, Arthur, as you saw yourself, had been behaving rather
wildly, and the inference is clear that he had been borrowing
money right and left. His debt, of 200 pounds to which he alluded,
was, as I have ascertained, a matter of mere bluff to obtain
money from you to pay a gambling debt. But he could not get it
from you, and he was in despair."

"It is unfortunately true. But you must listen to the whole
story. You remember that I examined the outside of your house
yesterday. I observed that the snow lay deep in the lane, but
that it was broken in one place by a track of feet. It was the
foot of a man, and it was certainly not your son's, since he
wore no shoes. I measured the track. It was that of a man of
imposing size, tall and heavy. There were other things, also,
which drew my attention. I observed that the snow was not
broken between the door and the spot where the man stood, showing
that he had not approached from that side. He had gone, then,
round from the side lane. I also saw that one of your lower
window-sills was smeared with wet mud, although the ground in the
garden was quite dry. Finally, I found that the wooden case
containing your coronet was smeared with the same mud, though
there was no mark of mud in the dressing-room itself. The
conclusions which I drew from these facts were: that the man had
passed through the side lane; that he had reached the window by
stepping onto a ledge of the kitchen door, which ledge was, as
you have said, smeared with mud; and that he had left the case
upon the sill, and had broken it open in the kitchen."


"As impossible as that your son should have stolen the gems. And
yet it is so. This is the true explanation of the mystery. It
was Sir George Burnwell who planned the whole thing. He knew that
your son was in debt and that he would be likely to ask you for
money. He also knew that you were anxious to see Arthur happily
married to your niece. He came to your house that night.  He knew
the secret of the bureau, having discovered it when he was a
frequent visitor.  He knew that your son was susceptible to his
influence, and that Miss Holder was very devoted to her cousin.


"It is perfectly true. I have proofs which would convince you,
were it worth while to go into them, that they had a secret
understanding and that she has run away with him. That is one
reason why she left your house this morning, for she had
arranged to be near him and to await him there."

"And the gems?"

"The gems were merely used to make the flight more easy and
secure. Your son, Arthur, was in love with Miss Mary Holder, but
she had refused him. He was in great financial trouble. Sir George
Burnwell, having heard of the coronet, proposed to your son that
he should break off a corner, take the three beryls, and then
substitute a false one which would easily deceive the eye. The
whole thing, to him, was a joke, an exciting game, and his desire
to settle his debts was the motive which influenced him. It is
easy to suppose that Sir George and your niece had concerted a
plan to make good their escape in the confusion of the night."

"But the gems were not on Arthur, and yet he was not able to
conceal them?"

"No, they were not on Arthur. They are in the possession of Sir
George. At the time that your son removed a gem, Sir George
and your niece were watching, and the moment that the deed was
done the gems were passed out of the window to them. As soon as
your son had returned to his room, they went out to the stable
lane, and having made good their escape into the country, they
have never since been heard of. The coronet was broken by your
son, but only because Sir George had shown him how it could be
done with such ease."

"And Lucy Parr?"

"She saw them go and was herself an accomplice to their flight.
I have already arrested her, and this is the boot which she left
behind her."

"But the noise, Mr. Holmes! The noise that I heard!"

"That was caused by the passing out of the gems, not by your son
breaking off the corner."


"It is unfortunately only too true. I have had the greatest
difficulty in getting proof of it, for she is as clever as she is
beautiful. However, there was one little thing which she
overlooked."

"What was that?"

"The fact that her sweetheart, the green-grocer, has a wooden
leg, and that he must have stood a little way from the kitchen
door while he waited to receive the gems. Now, you will notice
that there was no snow upon his path, whereas there was a good
deal upon the path which leads from the front door round to the
kitchen door. Therefore, he must have come to the house by the
front, not by the side, and so, of course, could not have
carried the gems past your window, for the reason that there was
no snow on that part of his path."

"It is unfortunately more than possible; it is certain. Neither
you nor your son knew the true character of this man when you
admitted him into your family circle. He is one of the most
dangerous men in England--a ruined gambler, an absolutely
desperate villain, a man without heart or conscience. Your niece
knew nothing of such men. When he breathed his vows to her, as he
had done to a hundred before her, she flattered herself that she
alone had touched his heart. The devil knows best what he said,
but at least she became his tool and was in the habit of seeing
him nearly every evening."

"I cannot, and I will not, believe it!" cried the banker with an
ashen face.

"Burnwell had then gone round to the tradesman's entrance,
knowing that the key was never removed from the kitchen door, and
had slipped in there. He had, as you saw, a wooden leg, and,
being a man of great strength, had no difficulty in forcing the
bureau lock and in breaking off a corner of the coronet. He took
the three gems, handed them to your niece, and then got safely
away before your son appeared upon the scene. Your son, aroused
by the noise, came to see what was the matter. He saw the open
bureau and the broken coronet. He picked it up to see if any gems
were missing, and, finding none, tried to repair the damage. As
he was doing this, you awoke and made a scene. He would not
incriminate his cousin Mary, so he kept silence. Thus the facts
lie."

"Sir George Burnwell, finding that his plans were threatened,
waited until the house was quiet, and then, having gained access
to your room, probably by the aid of your son's key, which he may
have stolen or borrowed from the careless youth, he opened your
bureau, took out the coronet, and, after wrenching off one of
the corners with his powerful hands, hid the gems somewhere,
returning the coronet to its place. You were awakened by the
noise of his movements, and rushed in just in time to see your
son bending over the coronet which he had himself picked up in
order to examine it."

"Sir George, meanwhile, had crept round to the tradesmen's entrance,
which is, as you know, seldom used, and which is concealed from the
road by the high hedge. He had concealed himself in the shrubbery,
and when all was quiet he had slipped into the house, had
unfastened the bureau, had removed the three gems, and had
returned in the same way."

"But my son?"

"Your son, as you know, has always had a key to your bureau.
Finding the coronet missing, and in his desperation to get the
money for his debts, he had come down to get the rest of it. He
had not touched it, I believe, when you surprised him."

"But his silence!"

"I have told you that he was desperate and angry. He would not
betray his cousin."

"But the gems were loose in the case. Surely, they would have fallen out when he handled it."

"That was his cleverness, Mr. Holder. There was no need for him
to handle them at all. When Sir George handed the three stones
over to your niece, it was she who loosened them from the setting.
That explained their being loose. All she had to do was replace
the empty setting. It was the neatest bit of work I have ever
seen. It shows the hand of a woman."

"Meanwhile, Sir George, having got possession of the key, had
already opened the bureau and had removed the coronet. He had
probably listened at the door, and knew that you were going to
examine the house. As soon as you were safely upstairs, therefore,
he returned to the drawing-room window, took the coronet from
his pocket, and placed it, with the missing gems, upon the table
before he disappeared again into the night. This part of his
plan, however, was never carried out. At the last moment your son
entered the room, and, finding the coronet lying there, took it
up, and tried to straighten it, believing, as you and I now
believe, that it had been tampered with. That is all. I have
the man, the gems, and I think that you will not ask me for
more."

"Then, while you were upstairs, Burnwell, aided by Lucy Parr, whom
he had made his accomplice, entered the house, opened the bureau
with the key which your son had mentioned, and removed the gems.
They were in the act of escaping when Arthur, awakened by some
sound, came out into the hall. He saw Burnwell, and the two
struggled. In the scuffle the coronet was dropped, and one of its
corners bent. Burnwell escaped and got away with the stones.
Arthur, fearing, no doubt, that his father would suspect him of
having been in this affair, and not wishing to bring his father
into contact with this dreadful man, concealed the bent coronet
in his room, and has ever since refused to explain."

"But how did you find out?"

"Oh, that was easy enough. Your son is not a hardened villain. He
was only trying to save himself and his father from a much worse
scandal. But Burnwell is a far more experienced criminal. He is
a master of his art, but even he could not leave such footmarks
without betraying himself. I saw them--quite clearly."

"But where are the gems?"

"In Sir George Burnwell's possession, where, if I am right, they
will remain but for a short time. I have already informed the
police, and we can only wait the issue. Your son will be
liberated."


"Your boy, Arthur, went to bed after his interview with you but
he slept badly on account of his uneasiness about his club debts.
In the middle of the night he heard a soft tread pass his door,
so he rose and, looking out, was surprised to see his cousin
walking very stealthily along the passage until she disappeared
into your dressing-room. Petrified with astonishment, the lad
slipped on some clothes and waited there in the dark to see what
would come of this strange affair. Presently she emerged from the
room again, and in the light of the passage-lamp your son saw
that she carried the precious coronet in her hands. She passed
down the stairs, and he, thrilling with horror, ran along and
slipped behind the curtain near your door, whence he could see
what passed in the hall beneath. He saw her stealthily open the
window, hand out the coronet to someone in the gloom, and then
closing it once more hurry back to her room, passing quite close
to where he stood hid behind the curtain.

"It is not only possible, but certain. I have Sir George's
testimony to that effect, together with the evidence of the cut
upon his forehead, which I found as I described to you in the
stable lane. The gems were found, as I expected, in the pocket
of the coat which the villain had thrown off in his flight. It is
a very pretty little problem, and I am pleased to have had the
opportunity of looking into it. The evidence against your son
was so strong that it was only by the merest chance that I was
able to clear him. I shall write a short account of this
extraordinary case for the benefit of the police department."

"God bless you, Mr. Holmes!" cried the banker, rising from his
chair and wringing my companion's hand. "You have saved my
honour, you have saved my son's career, and you have prevented
the worst of all scandals."

"It is an admirable case," said Holmes, smiling. "It is to my
mind, one of the most interesting that I have had in my career.
There is the singular coincidence of the two wooden legs. And then
the question of the noise which woke you. I assure you that the
snapping of that gold corner would have made a sound louder than
a pistol shot. It was a matter of physical impossibilities,
which always appeal so much to me. The young lady's note was, of
course, a mere blind to draw our attention from the real state of
the case."

"It was certainly all very baffling," I remarked.

"Yes. It was certainly very puzzling. The main thing was that I
should find the man with the wooden leg."

"Sir George Burnwell?"

"Precisely. He was not difficult to find when I knew where to
look for him."

"But how did you know where to look?"

"There were only two clues. The first was, that after hearing the
banker's story, I observed that the window was wide open. It
occurred to me that it might be possible to find some traces of
footmarks in the soft snow which covered the ground. The second
clue was in the fact that the young lady's note had referred to
her future being provided for. In my experience, a note of that
kind usually implies a prior understanding."

"Yes, you were fortunate in finding those clues."

"They were not difficult to find. It is the observation and
arrangement of the details which is the most difficult part. We
must now go and see what this unfortunate young gentleman has to
say for himself."
