"It is not only possible, but it is the strict and literal truth.
Your son, when he found that the gems were missing, naturally
concluded that Sir George Burnwell had dropped them in the scuffle
and that they were lying somewhere in the stable lane. He
searched for them, but in vain. Then he went back to the house,
and it was at that very instant that you awoke. The whole thing is
as clear as daylight. The gems I recovered this morning. It was
a very simple business to pick up the track. I had only to go to
the green-grocer's and find out which man was wanted, and then to
go along the lane to the spot where the struggle had taken
place. There were the three gems lying on the snow, and a small
quantity of blood from a cut upon Sir George's head. A shrewd
policeman, but not a shrewd enough one. The green-grocer, Francis
Prosper, was my assistant, and I hope that you will be able to
secure him on the charge of receiving stolen goods."

"And what is to become of Mary?"

"That I cannot tell. She will probably be hunted down. Burnwell
is a man who will not leave her to face the consequences."

"It is terrible!"

"It is sad, but inevitable. When once a woman has lost her
character, what is left for her to live for?"

"Do you really mean," said Mr. Holder, looking eagerly from the
gems to the detective, "that it was Sir George Burnwell who did
this dreadful deed?"

"There is no room for a doubt of it."

"And you say that Arthur is innocent."

"I am as certain of it as that we are now sitting here."

"Thank God!" ejaculated the financier. "Then it is not
impossible that all may yet be well."

"I would not say so much. Much has to be done before all is well
again, but, at least, the disgrace may be removed."

"Then there is only one other point."

"What is that?"

"Where did he get that 200 pounds which he asked for?"

"From Sir George Burnwell. He had received it that evening, and
it is likely that he only showed it in order to taunt and
irritate you. The rest is simple enough."

"You are a marvellous man, Mr. Holmes!"

"Elementary, my dear sir. Elementary!"

"It is not only possible, but it is the absolute truth. Your son
is as innocent of theft as I am. He had the coronet in his hands
it is true, but it was to replace it. When he saw that the corner
was broken off he attempted to conceal the injury to it by
straightening it. As to the missing gems, they are in Sir George
Burnwell's possession."

"But why did not Arthur explain this to the police?"

"Because he feared that it would implicate his cousin Mary, and
the scandal of the affair would be even worse than the loss of
the coronet. When he found that he was to be suspected of theft,
his pride revolted and he preferred to suffer any fate rather
than to betray the woman he loved."

"Good heavens! The noble fellow! But Mary?"

"She is now in the hands of Sir George Burnwell, and heaven help
her! I cannot say more than this, that there is a warrant out for
his arrest and that we shall do all that we can to get them back."

"Perfectly possible, and perfectly true. Your son, in a panic,
threw the coronet down and stood irresolute. He would have told
you all, but for your own violent and insulting language. It was
then that I came upon the scene. I found traces of a struggle
near the window, and also saw the marks of boots in the snow
which corresponded to the description given to me by Miss Holder.
These facts, when coupled with those which you have yourself
supplied, and with the knowledge that Sir George Burnwell was a
man who was capable of any crime, formed the basis of my
deductions. The three gems, I found embedded in the mud close
beside the window. I then went and examined the window itself,
and found that it had not been fastened in the usual way, the
catch being broken--a fact which I ascertained by comparing it
with the other windows of the house. Now I ask you what possible
motive your son could have for thus breaking the catch? The thing
is incredible, and it is inconceivable that he could have used
violence on the coronet for any purpose save to conceal what had
been done by others."

"It is not only possible, but it is the absolute truth. Sir George
Burnwell, finding that he had only secured three of the gems,
and that the coronet was damaged, determined to abandon the
enterprise. He knew that the police would look for him in his
own house, so he made his escape, leaving his accomplice to bear
the brunt of the affair. He did not attempt to conceal himself
far from Streatham, for he knew that he had only to wait a few
hours until he could safely return and take his flight with your
niece."

"But how did you find out all this?"

"You then roused his anger by calling him names at a moment when
he felt that he had deserved your warmest thanks. He could not
explain the true state of affairs without betraying one who
certainly deserved little enough consideration at his hands. He
took the more chivalrous view, however, and preserved her
secret."

"The inference was very natural, but you must admit that the
facts were entirely against him. The evidence pointed so clearly
to his guilt that it was difficult for the most experienced
detective to come to any other conclusion. The most extraordinary
part of the whole business is that, although the police have been
working at it day and night, they have not yet found the
missing stones."

"Where are they then, Mr. Holmes?"

"They are in the wooden leg of Mr. Francis Prosper. He is a
thorough villain, and the best of the lot. It was he who caused
the noise which awoke you last night by closing his window when he
had gone out and had taken the gems."

"It is not too late to make amends," said Holmes.  "And I think
that we may rely upon you, Mr. Holder, to make them handsomely.
The police will, I am sure, be only too glad to drop their
proceedings in the face of such a complete explanation.  I have
no doubt that Sir George Burnwell will find himself in a very
difficult position should he remain in England."


"He did go out. I found his track in the snow. It went down the
garden path, across the lawn, and through the hedge, but it did
not return. It led through the shrubbery to the road, and there
I found the other half of the coronet lying close to the wall.
There were traces of blood upon it, which accounted for the
wound upon Sir George's forehead.  He had evidently thrown it
away at once."

"Yes, and his silence. It was the silence of a man who is
covering up the disgrace of another rather than his own. Now, Mr.
Holder, you have a double duty to perform. You must get your son
out of prison, and you must take action to prevent this villain
from doing any more harm."

"The inference was very natural, Mr. Holder," said Holmes. "I
myself was completely deceived for some time. The three gems
were found embedded in the cut made by Arthur's heel, which he had
concealed under the loose earth in the lane."

"When I arrived at the house," continued Holmes, "I at once went
very carefully round it to observe if there were any traces in
the snow which might help me. I knew that none had fallen since
the evening before, and also that there had been a strong frost
to preserve impressions. I passed along the tradesmen's path, but
found it all trampled down and indistinguishable. Just beyond it,
however, at the far side of the kitchen door, a woman had stood
and talked with a man, whose round impressions on one side showed
that he had a wooden leg. I could even tell that they had been
disturbed, for the woman had run back swiftly to the door, as was
shown by the deep toe and light heel marks, while Wooden-leg had
waited a little, and then had gone away. I thought at the time
that this might be the maid and her sweetheart, of whom you had
already spoken to me, and inquiry showed it was so. I passed
round the garden without seeing anything more than random tracks,
which I took to be the police; but when I got into the stable
lane a very long and complex story was written in the snow in
front of me.

"I returned then to the house, examined the window, and found a
small piece of gold with three gems in it lying on the snow. It
had been thrown out from the window, as I judged by the direction
of the mark, and it was this which enabled me to offer you your
coronet once more. The rest was clear enough. Your son had told
you the truth as far as he could, but it was so fantastic that
you could not believe it. The gems which were missing from the
coronet had been those which Sir George had torn off in his
struggle with Arthur. That is all I can tell you for the present.
When you have seen your son again, perhaps you will have the
goodness to explain some other features of this very singular
case."

"I then examined the window, and found that the sill was smeared
with rust which could only have come from the heel-plates of a
heavy man's boot. It was an old pair of boots, as the rust showed,
and there was only one such pair in the house. The other
impression I found was from a naked foot. This was all that I could
discover at the time. I came back to the house and went upstairs
to your room. I looked at the coronet and concluded that the
piece must have been broken off by a sudden wrench, and also that
it must have made a loud snapping sound in the act. I then
examined the bureau, and found that it had a noiseless lock, so
that you could not have heard Arthur when he opened it. I
concluded that he had opened it, that he had seen his cousin
leave the house with the coronet, and that he had run after her
to try and save you from the consequences of her act."

"My poor boy!" cried the banker.

"He acted nobly," said Holmes. "I have already informed him that
the truth is known. He has now gone to join Mary and her lover."

"I then examined the window through which the coronet had been
passed. It was a small one, but it was open, and I observed that
the sill was covered with a fine layer of dust, except for one
small space, where the marks of a hand were very clear. I found
that there were no marks upon the window-ledge outside, so I
knew that the man had passed the coronet over, and not dropped it
through, or that the wind had not carried it away from the window,
as might have been the case, had the window been open a little
time. I noticed, further, that the snow upon the path was
untouched, except for the marks of the men whom I have
mentioned; and I concluded, therefore, that it must have been
passed, not thrown. Finally, I examined the bureau in which the
coronet was kept, and the cupboard in which the key hung, and I
found that the key was an ordinary one, that it was slightly
worn, and that no expert was required to open the bureau with it,
which went to show that an innocent person might have done it. I
then put the matter into order, and left the house."

"I then returned to the house, and examined the window through
which the coronet had been passed. I found that the snow had been
worn away from the sill, and there was the very faint impression
of a thumb or finger-mark upon the stone. It was, of course,
impossible to say who had been there, but I argued that if Sir
George Burnwell had taken the coronet from the inside, then he
would have had to make a noise which would certainly have roused
you; but if the maid had been there with her lover, the latter
would have found it impossible to break the coronet without
rousing you, and it was quite plain that your son had not done
it. This, therefore, left the theory that someone from the
outside had gained access to your room and taken the coronet. The
question was how.

"The window was closed; the door was locked; but there was, as
you saw, a third way of entering your room, namely, by the
dressing-table window. I went round to that window, and found a
small fragment of a torn envelope stuck on the top of the window
sill. This I took down and examined. It was a corner of a very
expensive notepaper, of which the address was already cut off,
but in the upper left-hand corner was a small piece of the coat-of-arms of the Beryl family. It bore the name of Sir George
Burnwell.

"That was how it was that I knew the guilty person. The fact that
he had cut the paper at the side and the exact size of the
missing triangle showed me that he had planned the crime and had
made the hole in the coronet to secure his prize."

"I returned to the house, examined the window, and found a
fragment of the coronet upon the sill. It had been torn off in
the struggle, and contained three stones. I then went upstairs,
examined the lock of your bureau, and satisfied myself that it was
a noiseless one. Your son's statement, that the bureau could be
opened with the key of the lumber-room cupboard, proved, when I
tested it, to be true. I did not wish to examine the coronet more
closely at the time, but I did ask you to break off the other
corner, so as to prove what a noise it would make. When I found
that it was too strong for me I felt certain that a man weaker
than myself could not have broken it off."

"On entering the house, however, I examined, as you remember, the
sill and framework of the hall window with my lens, and I could
at once see that someone had passed out. I could distinguish the
outline of an instep where the wet foot had been placed in coming
in. I was then beginning to be able to form an opinion as to what
had occurred. A man had waited outside the window; someone had
brought the gems; the deed had been overseen by your son; he had
pursued the thief; had struggled with him; they had each tugged
at the coronet, their united strength causing injuries which
neither alone could have effected. He had returned with the
prize, but had left a fragment in the grasp of his opponent. So
far I was clear. The question now was, who was the man and who
was it brought him the coronet?

"I then looked at the coronet itself and at the way in which the
corner had been broken off. It was clear to me that it could only
have been done by a powerful man. It was also clear that the thief
had been hurt, and that, therefore, it was not someone who could
run very swiftly. This fitted in with what I knew of Sir George
Burnwell's rather portly appearance and lack of athletic habits.
When I had cleared this part of the question, there was no longer
any difficulty in discovering the rest. It was clear that the
lover had been waiting, and that the woman had gone back to her
room and come down to him again. By now I felt pretty confident
that I had the whole thing, and I set off for London to find the
man."

"I then went round to the other side of the house, and, after a
little search in the snow, I found the other fragment of the
coronet, showing that the thief had dropped that piece also. This
was not far from the wooden thicket. I examined it carefully, and
found that it fitted in perfectly with the part which was already
in your possession. Then I knew that I had my man. When I saw the
boot in the lane I knew also the man. I went to his house,
found that he had been away the night before, and that he had
returned about four o'clock in the morning with mud upon his
boots. The boots themselves had holes in them. I asked the
question, 'Do you mind my looking at your boot?' 'Certainly,'
said he; and when I had looked at it and seen the shape of the
holes I felt positive that the man had passed out that window. I
then went to the other end of the town and found a bootmaker, who
told me that he had repaired a pair of such boots for Sir George
Burnwell only a few days before, and then I went to Sir George's
house, where I found him still in bed, but with a nasty cut on his
eye. That is all, Mr. Holder. Are there any other points?"

"I then looked at the coronet itself. It was twisted. Your son
had not twisted it, for he had not the strength. Neither had
your niece, for her hand is delicate. I therefore deduced that
the thief must be a man of exceptional strength. Only one man
could I think of in your circle who would combine the strength,
the wickedness, the audacity, and the knowledge of your affairs.
Sir George Burnwell was the only person who fitted the case."

"I then went to the stable lane, where I found a boot such as
Sir George Burnwell might have worn, and which was the size and
shape of the impressions in the snow. I also discovered that the
footmarks of the man in boots had been made by a man who was
carrying something heavy in his left hand. When I examined the
coronet I saw that the gold was bent, and that the small piece
which had been broken off had been twisted also. As this could
only have been done by a violent effort, and as your son is a
strong lad, I was sure that his story was correct.

"I then looked at the coronet itself, and observed that the
injured portion was such as might have been produced by a blow
from the fist, while the other portions showed that the gems had
been forced out by some instrument. Then I examined the lock of
your bureau, and, finding that it was a noiseless one, I knew
that the thief must have been someone who was thoroughly familiar
with the house. It was also obvious that the gems had been taken
away by someone who did not wish to be seen, or who was capable of
concealing them very cleverly. My conclusion, therefore, was that
your niece had been the guilty party and had given the gems to
Sir George Burnwell. Her motive, however, was not love of him, but
a sense of guilt and shame at what she had done."

"And who could it be who was her confederate? A lover evidently,
for who else could outweigh the love and gratitude which she must
feel to you? I knew that you went out little, and that your
circle of friends was a very limited one. But among them was Sir
George Burnwell. I had heard of him before as being a man of evil
reputation among women. It must have been he who wore those boots
and retained the missing gems. Even though he knew that Arthur
had discovered him, he might still flatter himself that he was
safe, for the lad could not say a word without compromising his
own family.

"That was I. I had no intention of allowing myself to be seen by
you. I have no doubt that the missing fragment of the coronet
is at Sir George's lodgings. I have every reason to believe that
he will take his departure from England to-day, or to-morrow at
latest."

"And Mary?" asked Mr. Holder, with a great sigh.

"She is safe. My knowledge of her character and of Sir George's
plans enabled me to find her and bring her to a place where she
is quite safe from his pursuit. She is one who may have erred, but
whose heart is still true to the instincts of honour and love.
Her behaviour, after all, is but the result of an impulsive
nature and of the influence of a great, and, for her, overwhelming
passion."


"Precisely. That was I. I went round to the back of your house and
saw that the window was open. I also saw the precious stones
lying on the grass outside. I had no difficulty in finding out
how they came there. Sir George, after the scuffle, had evidently
dropped them, and then, realizing that they were gone, he had
waited for a time in the lane until the alarm was given, and had
then slipped away quietly. Your son, I believe, is rather a better
athlete than Sir George, and no doubt he made for the highroad,
leaving him to pick up the jewels after he had gone."

"That was I. I then returned to Baker Street, changed my clothes,
and came here to have an interview with you, after which I went
down once more to Streatham and made myself acquainted with
various details, which I have already mentioned to you. I then
told your son the true story, showed him that the game was up, and
persuaded him to tell the truth to the police. Having got as far
as that I returned here to meet you, leaving him to confess
everything to them. I shall now, if you please, hand over the
missing gems. I should say that the green-grocer whom your niece
saw last night is a cousin of mine. He has a wooden leg and has
been very useful in many cases. When he had done me the service
of keeping the lane open for me, I sent him home."

"That was I. I then went round to the jeweller's, who is a friend
of mine, and showed him the missing piece. He at once recognised
it and said that it could be replaced, which I found was true
when I examined the broken portion. The three gems were found
loose in one of the boots, the other pieces being still in the
coronet. You will remember that Sir George remarked on the
difficulty of breaking off the part in question. Now, it was
broken off, but not by human strength, but by a blow from the
iron bar, such as Sir George carried with him, which I discovered
in his room. That is the whole story, my dear sir; a very
pretty one, is it not? Only, it seems that you have missed your
nephew more than your gems."

"Precisely. It was I. I had ascertained that Sir George was
going away to-day, and I wished to be on the spot to see him
before he departed. That is why I did not call at your house
yesterday. His valet told me that he had left his boots at the
cobbler's and had taken a pair of elastic-sides from the box in
his room. I have them here. I found them in a cupboard in Sir
George's bedroom. The gems were also inside. I think that is all."

"Precisely. It was I. I found that I had my man, so I came home
and changed my clothes. It was a delicate part which I had to
play then, for I saw that a prosecution must be avoided to avert
scandal, and I knew that so astute a villain would see that our
hands were tied in the matter. I went and saw him. At first, of
course, he denied everything. But when I gave him every
particular that had occurred, he tried to bluster and took down a
life-preserver from the wall. I knew my man, however, and I
clapped a pistol to his head before he could strike. Then he
became a little more reasonable. I told him that we would give
him a price for the stones he held--1000 pounds apiece. That
brought out the first signs of grief that he had shown. 'Why,
dash it all!' said he, 'I've let them go at six hundred for the
three!' I soon managed to get the address of the receiver who had
them, on promising him that there would be no prosecution. Off I
set to him, and after much chaffering I got our stones at 1000
pounds apiece. Then I looked in upon your son, told him that all
was right, and eventually got to my bed about two o'clock, after
what I may call a really hard day's work."

"I am afraid not," said Holmes, smiling.  "But I have every reason
to believe that she is safe, and, indeed, that she is in the best
possible hands.  She will find that even Sir George Burnwell has
his limitations."
"I fear not," said Holmes, smiling. "But she is safe, and I think
that she will find a way to make her peace with you in time.  She
has chosen her path, and it is not for us to judge her.  It is
enough that we have righted a great wrong, and that the Beryl
Coronet is once more safe in its place."
"I fear not," said Holmes, smiling. "But she is safe, and, I
think, happy.  She will not wish to return to you, Mr. Holder,
but you may rest assured that she is in no danger.  The game is
played, and the queen is off the board."
"I have a pretty shrewd idea," said Holmes, smiling, "but that is
a detail which does not concern the present case. I have no doubt
that Sir George will find her a most expensive companion. When
you have made your peace with your son, and when the first
shock of your great sorrow has passed away, it would be well for
you to think quietly over this matter, Mr. Holder. It may help
you to realize the true position which you occupy in the world of
finance when you discover that you are the most careless man in
England. Such carelessness is criminal."
"I can only suggest that you advertise in the agony columns of the
daily papers.  I have no doubt that she will see them, and that
she will then communicate with you. As to Sir George Burnwell,
he may be left to the vengeance of the law.  I have done all
that I could for you, Mr. Holder, and I trust that this great
public calamity has been averted."
"I think that we may safely say," returned Holmes, "that she is
wherever Sir George Burnwell is. It is equally certain, too, that
whatever her sins are, they will soon receive a more than
sufficient punishment."
